subject: maths

moments.title: Newton's method of fluxions
moments.body:
During the plague years, Newton (age 22-23) develops calculus. He calls derivatives 'fluxions' (rates of change of 'fluents'). He works out the fundamental theorem of calculus — that integration is the inverse of differentiation. He uses calculus to derive Kepler's laws from gravitation.

He does not publish. He shows his work privately to a few colleagues.
moments.takeaway: Newton has the calculus by 1666. He shares it with no one publicly for 20 years.

moments.title: Leibniz invents calculus independently
moments.who: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Hanover and Paris
moments.body:
Leibniz, working in Paris and Hanover, develops his own version of calculus. His notation — dx, dy, the integral sign — is far cleaner than Newton's dot notation. He publishes in 1684 (differential calculus) and 1686 (integral calculus).

His papers reach Europe quickly. Mainland mathematicians adopt the Leibniz notation. Britain, loyal to Newton, sticks with fluxions — and falls behind by a century in mathematical analysis.
moments.takeaway: Notation matters. Leibniz's notation makes calculus learnable; Newton's doesn't.

moments.title: The priority dispute
moments.body:
A Swiss mathematician (Nicolas Fatio de Duillier) accuses Leibniz of plagiarism in 1699. The Royal Society investigates and finds for Newton in 1712 — but the committee was hand-picked by Newton, who also (anonymously) wrote much of the final report.

Leibniz dies in 1716, his reputation in tatters in Britain. Mainland Europe continues to credit him. The bitterness lasts decades.

quote.text: The mathematicians of the continent... judge after the Latin method, that he who first published this method to the world ought to be acknowledged the inventor.

moments.takeaway: Both invented calculus independently. The priority dispute poisons British and Continental mathematics for generations.

moments.title: Rigorous foundations — Cauchy and Weierstrass
moments.body:
Newton and Leibniz used 'infinitesimals' — quantities smaller than any positive number but not zero — which were philosophically suspect. Berkeley's 1734 'The Analyst' attacked them as 'ghosts of departed quantities'.

Cauchy and later Weierstrass replace infinitesimals with limits, defined rigorously by epsilon-delta arguments. Calculus becomes mathematically respectable.
moments.takeaway: It took 150 years to put calculus on a rigorous foundation. The intuition came first; the rigor came later.

now.title: Calculus today
now.body:
Calculus underpins almost all of physics, engineering, economics, biology and computer science. We use Leibniz's notation universally. Newton's fluxion notation appears only in physics (for time derivatives) and a few corners of differential geometry.

Extensions: calculus of variations, functional analysis, distribution theory, non-standard analysis (which rehabilitates infinitesimals rigorously), stochastic calculus (essential for finance and physics).
now.open_questions: Can we automate calculus? (Computer algebra systems like Mathematica do most undergraduate calculus already.) Are there number systems richer than the reals that would simplify analysis? Does the universe really require continuous mathematics, or are we missing a discrete version?

reflection: Newton was a vindictive man who used his position to crush opponents. Leibniz was a diplomat with broad interests who often spread himself thin. Newton's bias-laden 'investigation' was accepted as truth in Britain for over a century. How does institutional power distort what science records about its founders?
